final_answer: No. Under Texas law the trial court most likely did not err (and certainly did not clearly abuse its discretion, the mandamus standard) in disqualifying Smith Fullingham. Governing rule: Texas courts disqualify a firm over a nonlawyer (legal assistant/paralegal) who switched sides under a two-presumption framework (Phoenix Founders v. Marshall; National Medical Enterprises v. Godbey; In re American Home Products; In re Columbia Valley; In re Turner, 542 S.W.3d 553 (Tex. 2017)). (1) Presumption one: a nonlawyer who actually worked on the matter at the prior firm is irrebuttably presumed to have obtained confidences. Jones did substantial work for Apex for roughly two years (documents, hundreds of privileged communications, strategy meetings), so this is satisfied, and her claimed lack of recollection does not rebut it. (2) Presumption two: the nonlawyer is presumed to share confidences with the new firm. That presumption is rebuttable, but only by showing the firm took sufficient prophylactic measures: at a minimum, instructing the nonlawyer not to work on or discuss the matter and formal, institutionalized screening measures making contact with the file less likely. It becomes irrebuttable where the nonlawyer actually worked on the same matter at the new firm for the opposing side, or where the firm failed to take the required measures. Here Jones worked on the very same dispute for the opposing side thirteen times and e-filed two documents under her name, and the firm did not even ask about her history, admonish her, or screen her until after Apex complained in 2023. Decisive recent authority: In re Zaidi, No. 24-0245 (Tex. Apr. 10, 2026), whose facts closely track these (Prestige Consulting a relator; legal assistant previously with opposing counsel; hired years before the conflict arose; e-filing notices bearing her name; motion to disqualify filed about two months after discovery). The Court, per the available summaries, held that a firm must instruct a nonlawyer, at or before the time she begins work on a conflicted matter (even if the conflict arises long after hiring and regardless of whether she was hired as a side-switcher), not to work on any matter she worked on in prior employment, and must adopt formal, institutionalized screening; absent those, disqualification follows. It denied mandamus relief from a disqualification order. Waiver: Apex did not waive. Delay can waive a disqualification motion only if unreasonable and not explained; here Apex moved within about two months of learning of Jones's involvement in January 2023, and Zaidi held that e-filing notifications do not conclusively establish waiver as a matter of law (the notices in March 2022 do not impute knowledge to Apex). Smith Fullingham's post-hoc steps (assertion that Jones doesn't recall, hasn't shared information, will be screened going forward) are inadequate because screening must be in place before the nonlawyer begins work and the firm's responses were untimely; no screen can cure when she already worked on the matter. Caveats: I could not retrieve the full text of Zaidi or Turner (egress blocked), so details rest on search-result summaries of the opinions and on my background knowledge of the Phoenix Founders/Godbey line; pin cites should be checked. Also a trial court's disqualification is reviewed by mandamus for abuse of discretion, with no adequate appellate remedy for erroneous disqualification, but that deferential standard further favors affirming here.
